# Volume 4 — CHAPTER 17 A SEVEN GULLS WINTER

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Cold weather began intensely following New Year’s Day. Large, pale banks piled up around the small dwelling, and fronds of ice blanketed its glass panes. The ice in the harbor became firmer and denser, to the point that the residents of Seven Gulls commenced their customary winter journeys across it. The secure routes were marked with evergreen branches by a kindly Government, and both day and night the cheerful ringing of the sleigh-bells echoed across the frozen surface. When the moon shone at night, Nell listened to them inside her dwelling of fantasy as if they were magical bells. The gulf turned to ice, and the beam from the Seven Gulls light ceased to shine. Throughout the period in which shipping was halted, Captain Saul’s position required no work.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0000 }

“My companion, the First Mate, and I have no duties until spring other than staying warm and entertaining ourselves. In the past, the lighthouse keeper routinely relocated to the Glen during the winter months; however, my preference is to remain at the Point. At the Glen, there is a risk that the First Mate could ingest poison or be attacked by dogs. Admittedly, it is somewhat solitary without the light or the water to keep us company, yet provided our friends visit us frequently, we will manage until the season passes.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0001 }

Captain Saul owned an ice boat, and with him, Hugh and Nell and Lorna enjoyed numerous wild, glorious spins across the smooth harbor ice. Nell and Lorna also went on long snowshoe tramps together, traversing the fields, crossing the harbor following storms, or trekking through the woods past the Glen. In their walks and their chats by the fireside, they proved to be very good comrades. Both had something to offer the other—both considered life richer because of friendly sharing of thought and friendly silence; both gazed across the white fields separating their homes with a pleasant awareness that a friend was on the other side. Yet, regardless of all this, Nell sensed that a barrier constantly stood between Lorna and herself—a constraint that was never entirely gone.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0002 }

“I have no idea why it is impossible for me to draw nearer to her,” Nell remarked to Captain Saul one night. “My affection for her is so great—my admiration for her is so deep—it is my DESIRE to welcome her fully into my heart and slip directly into hers. Yet I am utterly unable to pass the boundary.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0003 }

“Mistress Carrow, your whole life has contained too much happiness,” Captain Saul remarked in a reflective manner. “That, I believe, explains the inability of you and Lorna to achieve true closeness in your spirits. Her history of grief and hardship forms the obstacle that separates you both. She bears no blame for it, nor do you; yet it remains, impassable to either of you.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0004 }

“Prior to my arrival at Grey Shutters, my early years were not particularly joyful,” stated Nell, as she looked quietly through the window toward the quiet, gloomy, lifeless elegance created by the shadows of bare trees casting themselves upon the snow in the light of the moon.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0005 }

“Perhaps that isn't so—nevertheless, it merely amounted to the customary misery of a youngster lacking somebody to care for them adequately. No TRAGEDY has occurred throughout your existence, Mistress Carrow. Conversely, nearly ALL of poor Lorna’s has consisted of tragedy. I suppose she senses, even if she is scarcely aware of the feeling, that a huge portion of her existence lies beyond your ability to access or comprehend—consequently forcing her to prevent you from reaching it—keeping you at a distance, as it were, to avoid being injured by you. You are aware that whenever we possess a tender spot on ourselves, we flinch away from anybody touching it or coming close. In my opinion, this applies to our spirits just as much as our physical forms. Lorna’s spirit has to be almost raw—so it is hardly surprising that she keeps it concealed.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0006 }

“Were that truly everything, Captain Saul, it wouldn’t bother me. It would make sense to me. Yet at certain moments—not continuously, but from time to time—I am nearly forced to think that Lorna doesn’t—doesn’t care for me. On occasion I catch an expression in her eyes that appears to reveal bitterness and aversion—it vanishes so fast—yet I have witnessed it, I am certain of that. And Captain Saul, it causes me pain. Being disliked is not something I am accustomed to—and I have striven so earnestly to gain Lorna’s affection.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0007 }

“You have earned it, Mistress Carrow. Do not entertain any silly idea that Lorna does not care for you. Were that the case, she would not interact with you at all, let alone be as friendly with you as she is. I am too familiar with Lorna Vane not to be certain of it.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0008 }

“The initial occasion I ever beheld her, herding her geese down the slope on the date I arrived at Seven Gulls, she gazed at me with that identical look,” Nell insisted. “I sensed it, even while I was marveling at her loveliness. She gazed at me with resentment—she truly did, Captain Saul.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0009 }

“Mistress Carrow, the ill feeling had to be over a different matter, and you merely received a portion of it since you chanced to walk by. Lorna TRULY has gloomy moods once in a while, the poor girl. Knowing what she is forced to endure, I am unable to fault her. The reason it is allowed is beyond me. Though the doctor and I have held many conversations regarding where evil comes from, we still have not fully uncovered everything about it. Life contains a great deal of incomprehensible matters, does it not, Mistress Carrow? At times events appear to turn out very fittingly, just as it happened for you and the doctor. On the other hand, everything appears to turn completely topsy-turvy. Take Lorna, who is so bright and lovely that one would consider her destined to be a queen, but she is confined over there instead, deprived of nearly every single thing a woman would treasure, possessing no future beyond serving Rufus Vane her entire existence. Mind you, however, Mistress Carrow, I venture to say she would select her present existence, modest as it may be, instead of the existence she endured alongside Rufus prior to his departure. THAT topic is a matter an awkward old sailor’s speech should not touch upon. You have given Lorna great assistance, though—she has become an altered person since your arrival at Seven Gulls. We who are her longtime friends observe the change in her, which you are unable to see. Miss Winifred and I were discussing the matter recently, and it represents one of the extremely few issues where we hold identical views. Therefore, simply discard any notion that she harbors dislike toward you.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0010 }

Nell could scarcely ignore it entirely, because there were certainly moments when she sensed, through an intuition that reason could not defeat, that Lorna nursed a strange, unexplainable bitterness toward her. Sometimes, this hidden awareness spoiled the joy of their friendship; other times it was nearly out of mind; yet Nell was constantly aware that the concealed spike remained, ready to pierce her whenever. She received a harsh wound from it the day she informed Lorna about what she anticipated the spring would yield for the little house of dreams. Lorna stared at her with harsh, resentful, hostile eyes.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0011 }

“So you are to have THAT, too,” she uttered, her voice strangled. Then, not saying another word, she swung around and walked over the fields toward home. Nell was profoundly pained; at that instant, it seemed to her that she could never care for Lorna again. However, when Lorna visited a couple of nights afterward, she behaved in such an agreeable, warm, candid, amusing, and engaging manner that Nell was captivated into pardoning and forgetting. Nevertheless, she did not ever speak of her cherished wish to Lorna again, and Lorna also never brought it up. Even so, one night, when late winter was waiting to hear the call of spring, she walked over to the small house to have a twilight conversation; and as she departed, she deposited a little, white box upon the table. Nell discovered it once she had departed and unsealed it in astonishment. Inside it lay a minuscule white gown of superb craftsmanship—fine embroidery, amazing tucks, pure beauty. Each stitch throughout it had been done by hand, and the small lace ruffles located at the collar and cuffs consisted of genuine Valenciennes. Resting upon it was a card—“with Lorna’s love.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0012 }

“She must have spent so many hours working on it,” Nell said. “Plus, the fabric probably cost a lot more than her budget actually allowed. She is so sweet to do this.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0013 }

Yet Lorna proved sharp and brief upon receiving Nell’s gratitude, causing the latter to feel once more turned inward.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0014 }

Lorna’s present was not the only one inside the small home. Miss Winifred had temporarily stopped making clothes for eighth infants who were neither desired nor welcomed, turning instead to stitching for a first child who was eagerly awaited and whose reception would be all that could be wished. A pair of extraordinary garments arrived from Cressida Hale and Isolde Duckett, one from each; while Mrs. Agatha Sowerby dispatched a few, where fine fabrics and sturdy needlework replaced lace and decorative borders. Nell personally crafted a great deal of them, untouched by any mechanical device, devoting to their creation the most joyful moments of that joyful winter.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0015 }

The small house had no visitor more regular or cherished than Captain Saul. Nell’s affection for the pure-hearted, genuine old mariner grew with each passing day. He possessed the invigorating quality of an ocean wind and the fascination of an old historical text. Listening to his tales never bored her, while his peculiar observations and notes gave her endless pleasure. Captain Saul belonged to that exceptional and captivating group of individuals who “never speak but they say something.” Within his nature, the essence of human compassion and the cunning of the snake blended in captivating measure.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0016 }

No circumstance appeared capable of unsettling Captain Saul or dampening his spirits in the slightest degree.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0017 }

“I’ve sort of acquired a pattern of enj’ying things,” he stated one time, after Nell had made a remark about his constant good humor. “It’s become so persistent that I think I even enj’y the unpleasant things. It’s wonderful entertainment believing they are unable to endure. 'Old rheumatiz,’ says I, whenever it clutches me severely, 'you’ve GOT to cease aching eventually. The harsher you are the quicker you’ll cease, perhaps. I am destined to overcome you eventually, either inside the body or outside of the body.’”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0018 }

Beside the fire at the lighthouse one evening, Captain Saul’s “life-book” was seen by Nell. Requiring no persuasion to display it, he handed it to her to read with pride.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0019 }

“I composed it for little Joe to inherit,” he remarked. “The thought of all my deeds and sights being entirely forgotten once I embark on my final voyage displeases me. As for Joe, he will keep it in mind and recount the tales to his offspring.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0020 }

The volume was bound in aged leather and contained the log of his travels and exploits. Nell considered what a wealth of material it might offer a writer. A valuable insight was contained in each sentence. By itself, the work possessed no artistic value; the captivating narrative ability of Captain Saul deserted him whenever he took up a pen; his famous stories were reduced to roughly scribbled outlines, and he suffered from terribly flawed spelling and grammar. Nevertheless, Nell believed that if an individual with true talent were given that plain account of a courageous, daring existence—interpreting the understated text to uncover the stories of hazards bravely confronted and obligations courageously fulfilled—an extraordinary tale could be crafted from its pages. Deep humor and intense sorrow were both concealed within Captain Saul’s “life-book,” awaiting the skill of a gifted storyteller to evoke the amusement, sorrow, and dread of a vast audience.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0021 }

Nell mentioned a portion of this to Hugh while the two of them walked toward home.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0022 }

“Why do you not give it a shot on your own, Nell?”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0023 }

Nell gave a shake of her head.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0024 }

“No. Only I wish it were possible for me. But my talent does not encompass it. Hugh, you are aware of my specialty—the imaginative, the whimsical, the attractive. One ought to possess a command of a forceful yet delicate manner of expression, be a sharp psychologist, a natural humorist, and a natural tragedian in order to compose Captain Saul’s biography as it ought to be done. An unusual blend of talents is required. Were Cedric older, he might manage it. In any case, my intention is to request that he travel here next summer to be introduced to Captain Saul.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0025 }

“Travel to this coast,” Nell penned in a letter to Cedric. “I fear that Nora, the Golden Lady, or the Twin Sailors cannot be located here by you; nevertheless, a single aged mariner who is able to share marvelous tales will be found by you.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0026 }

Cedric, nevertheless, replied in writing, expressing his regret that he would be unable to make the visit that year. His plans involved traveling overseas to pursue two years of study.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0027 }

“Upon my return, my beloved Teacher, I shall visit Seven Gulls,” was his written message.
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0028 }

“However, in the time that passes, Captain Saul ages,” Nell remarked mournfully, “and no person exists to record the story of his life.”
{: #nw-v04-c17-p0029 }
